definition: A camera roll — rotating the camera on its long (view) axis while the lens keeps pointing the same direction, i.e. a Dutch-angle tilt animated over time rather than held static — is used specifically to unsettle the viewer's own equilibrium, distinct from a pan (yaw) or tilt (pitch); it is used to match a character's physical disorientation, to signal a villain's ascent, or to visually enact a reversal of power partway through a single shot.
purpose: Give the camera a third, distinct rotational register (roll) beyond pan/yaw and tilt/pitch, reserved specifically for disequilibrium and power dynamics rather than ordinary framing or following.
visible_effect: The horizon line itself visibly tilts and rotates within the frame, unlike a pan or tilt where the horizon stays level — the world appears to rotate around the subject rather than the camera simply redirecting its attention.
psychological_or_gameplay_effect: Disorienting and unsettling by design ("disorienting, unsettling our equilibrium"); used to match a character's own panic or vertigo, to make a villain's rise to power visually unsettling, or — in the video's own Dark Knight example — to physically enact within a single shot a character's shift from powerless (strung upside down) to back in control, as the camera rolls to bring them upright relative to the frame.
physical_interpretation: Directly exploits the viewer's own vestibular/visual expectation that a level horizon means a stable, oriented world — rolling it violates that expectation the same way real disorientation (vertigo, being upside down, a fall) would.
use_cases: matching a character's own physical disorientation or panic
visually marking a villain's ascent or a morally unsettling turn

enacting a power reversal WITHIN a single continuous shot, so the reversal itself is felt rather than only stated (the video's own Joker-strung-upside-down example: the roll itself performs the shift in who has the upper hand)
non_use_cases: ordinary reframing or following where a level horizon should be preserved — a pan or tilt covers that case; rolling for a routine reframe would read as an unintended, distracting disorientation
interactions: dolly_push_vs_optical_zoom_perceptual_distinction and dolly_zoom_coordinated_invariant_effect (this same video) — together with roll, these establish the video's fuller catalogue of distinct camera registers, each reserved for a different narrative register rather than being interchangeable ways to "move the camera"
cadence_representation: A camera roll is already fully representable in Cadence's existing model: the camera item's `@origin` track is a CFrame carrying rotation on all three axes, so animating roll specifically (rotation about the view/forward axis, independent of pan/tilt) requires no new capability — `set_keyframe`/`get_rotation_degrees` already handle it exactly as they would any other rotation. What Cadence's own knowledge does not carry is the NARRATIVE association this video supplies: that roll specifically (as opposed to pan or tilt) reads as disorientation/power-reversal, worth recording since nothing in this build's `ai/vocabulary.js` or camera-related documentation currently distinguishes the THREE rotational registers by their typical narrative use.
control_surface: `set_keyframe` on the camera's `@origin` CFrame rotation component (roll/Z-axis specifically); `get_rotation_degrees` to inspect it.
detection_and_measurement_methods: `ai/motion.js sampleMotion`/`get_rotation_degrees` can already report a camera item's rotation about any axis, including roll specifically, over time — the MEASUREMENT already exists; nothing currently classifies a rotation as "a roll" versus "a pan" or "a tilt" by which axis dominates, though that classification would be a straightforward addition given the existing per-axis rotation data.
generation_or_modification_methods: `set_keyframe`/`set_easing` on the rotation component as usual; nothing currently generates a roll specifically as a named, distinct authoring action separate from an arbitrary rotation keyframe.
failure_modes: rolling the camera during an ordinary reframe with no disorientation/power-shift intent, producing an unintended unsettling effect
using a pan or tilt where a roll's specific disequilibrium register was actually wanted, understating the intended disorientation
roblox_considerations: A Roblox camera's CFrame carries full 3D rotation identically to Cadence's own model; a roll is simply rotation about the camera's own look-vector axis, native to the engine with no special support needed.
examples: "A roll turns the camera on its long axis while maintaining the direction of the lens... disorienting, unsettling our equilibrium" (video @ 15:47–15:54)

the Dark Knight example, confirmed in this session's own frame read of the labeled "CAMERA ROLL" shot showing the Joker strung upside down then righted as the camera rolls: "as the camera slowly rolls over he reveals that he still has the upper hand" (video @ 17:12–17:16)
